entities.name: Aulus Hirtius
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Aulus Hirtius, a Roman statesman, general, and historian, served as consul of the Roman Republic in 43 BCE, a tumultuous year following the assassination of Julius Caesar. Born into a plebeian family, his career was inextricably linked to Caesar, whom he served as a legate during the Gallic Wars and later as a trusted aide. His pivotal role in the post-Caesar power struggles, culminating in his death at the Battle of Mutina, positioned him as a significant, albeit short-lived, player in the transition from Republic to Principate. Hirtius is also remembered for his literary contributions, particularly his completion of Caesar's commentaries, which offer invaluable insights into Roman military and political life.

Hirtius's military acumen was honed under Caesar, participating in the Siege of Alesia in 52 BCE and other campaigns that solidified Roman control over Gaul. His diplomatic skills were also considerable, serving as an intermediary between Caesar and Pompey during the civil war. After Caesar's assassination in 44 BCE, Hirtius, initially aligned with Mark Antony, eventually joined forces with the Senate and Octavian (the future Augustus) against Antony. As consul, he led senatorial forces alongside his colleague Gaius Vibius Pansa Caetronianus and Octavian, decisively defeating Antony's legions at the Battle of Mutina in April 43 BCE. This victory, however, came at the cost of Hirtius's life, as he was killed in action during the fighting.
